evidence.excerpt: This book will help you find the weak part instead of blaming “AI” as though it were one indivisible object. Read the chapters in order to build the complete picture. Use the separate Concept Index when you need to look up one term—such as token, context, memory, routing or agent—and then jump to the chapter where that term does real work.

This is the first lesson of the whole book: the quality of an AI result depends on more than the wording of one prompt. It depends on what the system is trying to help you do, what information reached it, what operations ran, what the model produced and what you checked before acting.

Later chapters will open each part carefully: how models are trained and run; how tokens and context windows affect what fits; how session and memory differ; what retrieval, tools, permissions, routing and wrappers add; how agents and multi-step loops work; and why convincing answers can still fail. The Concept Index will let you find any one term without turning the book itself into a dictionary.

You did not consult one all-knowing thing. You used an **AI system**: the whole working arrangement that received your request and produced the result. That arrangement includes the product you opened, the instructions and material available for this task, at least one trained model, and the software that presents the answer. Some systems can also search, calculate, retrieve documents or take actions. The exact arrangement varies from product to product.

The **model** is an important part of that system, but it is not the whole system. It is the trained component that processes input and produces an output. The product and surrounding software shape what reaches it, which other capabilities are available and what you eventually see.
We will begin with one decision and follow it all the way through. Nothing floats around as a loose definition. Every part earns its name by changing what happens next.

Not every AI product has the same tools, and not every available tool runs on every request. The useful question is not “Does this AI have tools?” It is “What operation actually ran for this answer, and can I inspect what came back?”

1. **What decision am I actually trying to make?** If the system solved a narrower problem, restate the real one.
2. **What information did this answer actually use?** Check the messages, files, dates and missing facts that mattered.
3. **What current source or operation supports the consequential claims?** Inspect the returned evidence; do not treat fluency as a citation.
4. **What must remain my decision or another person’s responsibility?** Name the value judgment, permission or professional check that cannot be delegated.

evidence.excerpt: People and organisations using AI professionally have separate duties. Some concern systems that infer emotions from features such as a face or voice, called emotion recognition. Others concern systems that sort people into groups using such features—for example, estimating an age group from a face—called biometric categorisation. These names describe what the systems attempt to do; they do not guarantee that their conclusions are accurate.

“Europe’s AI transparency rules started on August 2. They require disclosure in particular situations, but an AI label tells you about origin, not whether the content is true. Think caller ID: useful before answering, no guarantee about what comes next.”

artifactEvidence.excerpt:
Last week’s Weekly asked how to tell a promise from proof. This week needs a sharper tool: read the verb.

An agency can study a safeguard. A legislature can enact a reporting duty. One chamber can pass a proposal. Investigators can report a campaign. A company can release a product. All are real developments, but they do not create the same protection, evidence or access.

California: study the switch, start the reporting

California’s September 18 executive order took effect immediately. It accelerated existing oversight work and set November 16 for recommendations on possible legal amendments, including independently checked shutoffs for advanced AI systems, onsite verifiers and broader incident reporting. It did not install a universal AI kill switch. The Electronic Frontier Foundation supports broader reporting and third-party investigations while warning that shutoff effectiveness remains active research and government control could threaten protected speech.

On September 21, California also made SB 1168 and AB 1577 law. They are two of seven data-centre bills signed that day; this Weekly does not claim to explain the other five. SB 1168 tells the utilities commission to assess opportunities for rate structures — the rules used to divide utility charges among customer groups — including data centres’ share of grid and procurement costs. An assessment is not an adopted tariff or a calculated household saving.

AB 1577 creates local and state reporting for covered data centres with at least 10 megawatts of electrical capacity. Its public releases must be anonymized and aggregated — combined so a public release does not expose one protected customer record — and its first specified statewide load-trend assessment belongs in the 2029 energy-policy report. Named public, research, safety, national-security, publicly owned and utility facilities are excluded from the cited reporting provisions.

Washington: a House vote is still a proposal

The US House passed H.R. 9340 by 417–3 on September 16. If enacted, it would require state regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider a standard for qualifying computing sites with at least 100 megawatts of peak demand. Under that standard, a large customer’s rate would recover the additional grid-upgrade cost needed to serve it.

The bill would require consideration and a determination; it would not itself set one nationwide retail rate. A September 17 unanimous-consent attempt in the Senate drew an objection. The current official sources in this packet do not establish a Senate vote or enactment. Your bill still depends on the relevant utility, regulator, project and approved rate design.

Card skimmers: an investigation, not your exposure notice

BleepingComputer reported on September 23 that security firm Gambit had investigated AI-assisted agents used in a retail card-skimming campaign. Gambit calls its underlying publication an interim report and separates recovered material and observed checks from estimates about scale and cost.

The consumer consequence is serious: card skimmers steal payment details from online stores. The evidence supplied here does not identify a complete victim list, establish that a particular reader’s card was taken or support a made-up instruction to cancel every card. Quantities and claims about the AI role remain attributed to the investigators until affected parties or independent evidence narrow the scope.

Product changes you may actually encounter

Anthropic said on September 16 that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. The practical change is that longer work can begin in an ordinary conversation rather than a separately chosen mode. The rollout starts with Pro and Max over several weeks; Team and Free are to follow, while Enterprise administrators get advance notice. Claude Docs and Slides are beta features on paid plans.

OpenAI also announced GPT-6 Sol and Luna in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users. Free and Go users can access Luna in the desktop app. The models were not yet available in Chat, and the company said rollout through the day could delay visibility. OpenAI says its performance and reliability comparisons come from its own evaluations, not independent proof that everyone should switch. For ordinary work, access and the task matter before a benchmark table does.

The week is not one story about AI speeding up or government catching up. It is a set of different decision chains. The California order leads to recommendations. The state laws lead to proceedings, reports and later public data. The House bill still needs enactment and local rate decisions. The security report needs corroboration or affected-party notices. Product releases still depend on plan, app and rollout.

For an electricity claim, look for the commission proceeding, local permit or approved rate. For a security claim, look for an affected retailer, issuer notice or updated investigation before assuming personal exposure. For a product announcement, check your plan and the surface named in the source: Work, Codex, Chat, desktop or another app are not interchangeable.

missingMechanism.observation: Each conclusion is preceded by its causal steps: enactment paths, rollout stages, and evidence chains are shown, not asserted.

genericAction.observation: Advice is case-specific: commission proceeding for electricity, issuer notice for cards, named plan and surface for products.

jargonBeforeMeaning.observation: Every technical term (rate structure, aggregated release, interim report, unanimous consent context) is explained at or near first use.

disconnectedSystem.observation: P003 explicitly links each actor to its downstream step, showing how effects move through each decision chain.

factlessConfidence.observation: Certainty is carefully bounded ('current official sources in this packet do not establish a Senate vote'); hedges match evidence throughout.

staleUnreviewableClaims.observation: Every time-sensitive claim carries its event date, and the closing note states the covered period and September 26 source refresh.

corporateSludge.observation: Prose is concrete and plain; no motivational or vague corporate language appears.

joylessInstruction.observation: Restrained but not dry: the verb-substitution device and direct second-person stakes keep human interest alive.

benchmarkNameDrop.observation: No communication benchmark or famous explainer is mentioned or leaned on.

curiosityWithoutPayoff.observation: The opening promise of a sharper tool is delivered in P004 and applied across all six developments.

familiarExampleWithoutTechnicalReturn.observation: Familiar anchors (bill, card, app) each return to the specific legal or rollout mechanism that governs them.

communicationPastiche.observation: Voice is original and consistent; no imitation of a known communicator's mannerisms.

entertainmentBeforeUnderstanding.observation: No humour or spectacle intrudes; understanding leads throughout.

mechanismCompressedBehindHook.observation: The hook is two short paragraphs; the causal explanation occupies the bulk of the piece with full development per section.

prematureClickBeforeMechanism.observation: Status conclusions ('still a proposal', 'not your exposure notice') are each backed immediately by the procedural steps that justify them.

inflatedTakeawayEnding.observation: P006 deliberately deflates: 'No new routine is compulsory'; the ending is narrower than the material, not grander.

purposeTooNarrow.observation: The piece covers all six developments in the supplied reader job and adds a transferable reading tool; no single task swallows the purpose.

mechanismBeforeMotivation.observation: The human reason (telling current duties from future decisions) is established in P001-P002 before any procedural machinery begins.

workedExampleOvertakesBookPurpose.observation: No single worked example dominates; the six items get proportionate space against the shared tool.

technicalExplainerVoice.observation: The organising perspective is the reader's exposure and access, not specialist taxonomy; procedure appears only where the reader's outcome depends on it.

factualReview.nextTrigger: Any later Senate action, enactment, California implementation, affected-party confirmation, correction, or rollout change.

claimMap.claim: California order directs recommendations, including possible statutory amendments.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: It did not install a universal AI kill switch.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The Government Operations Agency, in consultation with the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services, shall, no later than November 16, 2026, submit to my office recommendations, developed in consultation with national experts, addressing the technical feasibility and potential efficacy of amendments to existing state laws regarding AI safety and security, including at least the following:

EFF supports the focus on expanding reporting requirements under SB 53 for loss-of-control incidents, alongside third-party investigations. ... the effectiveness of kill switches in advanced AI systems remains an area of active research. ... government-controlled kill switches run the risk of being used as a form of retaliation against protected speech.

claimMap.scopeAndFreshness: Signed order and current EFF statement refreshed September 26; recommendation directive, not an installed universal switch.

claimMap.claim: California enacted selected data-centre reporting and assessment duties.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: An assessment is not an adopted tariff or a calculated household saving.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: As part of a new or existing proceeding, the commission shall assess opportunities for rate structures to do all of the following:

“Data center” does not include a facility with an electrical capacity of less than 10 megawatts. Beginning with the 2029 integrated energy policy report required pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 25302, and in subsequent biennial reports required pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 25302 thereafter as determined by the commission, the commission shall include an assessment of electrical load trends for data centers.
Governor Newsom today signed seven bills to strengthen California’s approach to data centers — requiring data centers to report about water and electricity use.

This section does not apply to a publicly funded research facility, public safety facility, publicly funded national security facility, publicly owned facility, or other utility facility, including, but not limited to, a facility operated for the purpose of providing telecommunications services to the public by a terrestrial facilities-based telecommunications, cable, or internet service provider.
The commission shall annually publish the information submitted pursuant to subdivision (b) in an anonymized and aggregated format on its internet website.

claimMap.scopeAndFreshness: SB1168 and AB1577 primary bill texts and the Governor’s count refreshed September 26. SB1168 directs an assessment, not a tariff; AB1577 contains the 10MW threshold, 2029 reporting assessment and stated exclusions. Article covers neither all seven bills nor a calculated household saving.
